890.title: The ban
890.hook: Antiochus IV outlaws Torah practice and defiles the Temple
890.tomorrow: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)
890.howItsDone: Jews remember the persecution under Antiochus at Hanukkah, when the Al HaNissim passage in the prayers recalls a wicked Greek kingdom that tried to make Israel forget the Torah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seventy-two elders in seventy-two rooms, all writing the same words. Your line was something always stays behind in the original. Did you thank a translator? Today, the meeting of two cultures turns into a law against one of them. Day eight hundred ninety.
screen: `SOMETHING ALWAYS STAYS BEHIND IN THE ORIGINAL.`

segments.voice: The order arrives in writing. The first book of Maccabees says the king, Antiochus, the one surnamed Epiphanes, writes to his whole kingdom that everyone should be one people, and each should give up their own laws. Then letters go to Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, with a list. No more offerings in the Temple. No more Sabbaths and festivals. No circumcising sons. Eat what the law forbids. And at the bottom, the penalty: whoever will not obey shall die. Officers are sent to make sure. It's a short paragraph in an old book. For a family in a village in Judah, it meant that keeping the Sabbath in their own home was now a crime.
screen: `ALL SHOULD BE ONE PEOPLE.` → `A LIST OF WHAT'S FORBIDDEN.` → `THE SABBATH BECOMES A CRIME.`

segments.voice: The book goes on, and it doesn't soften anything. In the Temple, on the altar, the king's men set up what the King James text calls "the abomination of desolation", an idol's altar where the altar of God had stood. Copies of the books of the law are found, torn to pieces, and burned. Women who circumcised their babies are put to death. Now, the important part: the book is honest that this pressure split the people. It says many in Israel went along, offered to idols and broke the Sabbath. And it says many others refused, held firm, and would not eat what the law forbade, even when refusing meant dying. Both groups were Jews, under the same pressure. This is not a story of good nations and bad nations. It's a story about what happens when a government decides that one way of life has to disappear. The rabbis later had a word for that kind of time: shmad, a time when practicing at all is forbidden. And the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, has a teaching for it: in an ordinary time, a person may break many commandments to save a life, but when a ruling power decrees against the faith, even a small custom becomes a line not to cross. One teacher's example is as small as changing a shoe strap. This is the doorway into the next few days. Tomorrow, a mother and her sons. After that, a priest in a small town who says no. And the holiday that grew out of all of it. But it starts here, with a list, and a king who wanted everyone to be the same.
screen: `THE ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION.` · `SOME WENT ALONG. SOME REFUSED.` · then, large: `SHMAD: WHEN PRACTICE IS FORBIDDEN.` · `EVEN A SHOE STRAP MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: value your freedom to practice. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of one thing you're free to do today because of what you believe or where you come from: light a candle, wear something, rest on a certain day, eat or not eat something, gather with your people, or choose no practice at all. Now imagine a letter arriving that forbids it, with a penalty at the bottom. Notice what rises in you. Then let the letter go, and come back to the plain fact: today, no such letter came. Hold that freedom gently, and spare a thought for anyone, of any faith, who did get the letter. If you pray, you can use words from your own tradition for them. The bell holds the time.
The ban. A king's written order outlawing Sabbath, circumcision and Torah, and an idol set on the Temple altar. Today's word.
Your line: freedom to practice. Today, do one small thing your tradition or your family asks of you, and do it on purpose, because you can. Day eight hundred ninety.

fork.reveal: 1 Maccabees is honest that the pressure split the people: many went along, and many others held firm and chose to die rather than break the covenant.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Maccabee story begins with a battle.

what a scholar hears: 1 Maccabees 1 lists the bans and admits many went along; the Talmud in Sanhedrin 74a–b calls such a time shmad and raises the stakes of even a small custom.

891.title: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)
891.hook: a mother encourages her sons to hold fast to their faith under torture
891.howItsDone: Jewish tradition remembers the mother and her seven sons as an example of kiddush ha-shem, sanctifying God's name, and some communities retell their story at Hanukkah and on Tisha b'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ban: a king's letter that made Sabbath, circumcision and Torah a crime. Your line was freedom to practice. What did you do on purpose, because you could? Today, one family meets that law face to face. Day eight hundred ninety-one.

A mother and seven brothers are brought before the king. The second book of Maccabees, chapter seven, tells it plainly. The order is simple: eat the forbidden meat, and live. One by one, the brothers refuse. The first to speak says: we are ready to die rather than break the laws of our fathers. The text does not hide what follows; one after another, the sons are tortured and killed, each refusing, each speaking a few last words about God, some about a life beyond this one. And through all of it there is one person in the room who has to watch every moment. The chapter turns its eyes to her.
screen: `A MOTHER AND SEVEN BROTHERS.` → `EAT, AND LIVE.` → `ONE BY ONE, THEY REFUSE.`

segments.voice: The text calls her marvelous above all, worthy of honorable memory. She sees her sons die in a single day, it says, and bears it with good courage because of her hope in the Lord. And she doesn't stay silent. She encourages each of them in the language of their fathers. Her words are about where life comes from: I don't know how you came to be in my womb. I didn't give you breath and life, and I didn't shape your body. The Creator of the world did, and in mercy, he will give you breath and life again. Then comes the hardest scene. Only the youngest is left. The king promises him riches and friendship if he'll turn, and asks the mother to talk him into it. She agrees to speak. She leans toward her son and, in the family language, says: have pity on me, who carried you nine months and nursed you three years. Look at the heaven and the earth. God made them out of nothing. Don't be afraid. Then, the text says, the youngest refuses too. And last of all, the mother dies. The rabbis told their own version of this story, in the Talmud, tractate Gittin, set in a different time. There, as the mother dies, a heavenly voice calls out a line from the Psalms. In the King James words: "a joyful mother of children." It's a strange, painful blessing. The story doesn't say she wasn't crushed. It says that in that room, she encouraged them.
screen: `MARVELOUS ABOVE ALL.` · `IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR FATHERS.` · `GOD WILL GIVE BREATH AGAIN.` · then, large: `A JOYFUL MOTHER OF CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to honor a brave parent. Sit quietly and let your breath settle. Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent, or anyone who raised you or stood beside you, who was brave in a hard moment. Maybe it was a hospital, a border, a job lost, a long illness, or a quiet choice nobody else saw. Picture their face, and let them be as they were, not perfect, just brave once. If no one comes to mind, think of a parent in your community, or the mother in today's story. Say their name inside, slowly. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to honor them. The bell holds the time.
Gittin, the Talmud tractate where the rabbis retold the mother and seven sons, ending with a joyful mother of children. Today's word.
Your line: she encouraged them. Today, say one encouraging sentence to someone facing something hard, in the language you share with them. Day eight hundred ninety-one.

match.prompt: the mother and seven sons — tap the pairs.

2 Maccabees 7 says she encouraged each one in the family tongue.
in 2 Maccabees, the mother dies before her sons

fork.setup: you're the mother. six sons are gone. the king promises your youngest riches if he turns, and asks you to persuade him. what do you say?
options: save yourself; do what the king says.
nothing at all; you can't bear to speak.

fork.reveal: she agrees to speak, then in the family language tells him not to fear. the king hoped she'd break him. she encouraged him.

original.note: Hebrew: a joyful mother of children, from Psalm 113:9, the line the heavenly voice calls out in the Talmud's telling.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about seven brave sons.
what it means: the chapter turns to the mother, who watches every moment and speaks courage to each son.
what a scholar hears: 2 Maccabees 7 tells it under Antiochus; the Talmud in Gittin 57b tells its own version in a different time, ending with Psalm 113:9.

892.title: Mattathias
892.hook: a priest in Modi'in refuses to sacrifice to idols, and the revolt begins
892.howItsDone: At Hanukkah, Jews add the Al HaNissim passage to their prayers, which names Mattathias son of Yohanan, the Hasmonean high priest, and his sons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother watched seven sons refuse, and spoke courage to every one, a story the Talmud retells in tractate Gittin. Your line was she encouraged them. Who did you encourage? Today, in a town outside Jerusalem, a priest says no out loud. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

Modi'in is a town, not the capital. The first book of Maccabees says a priest named Mattathias lives there with his five sons: John, Simon, Judas who is called Maccabeus, Eleazar and Jonathan. He has been mourning what's happening in Jerusalem, tearing his clothes, putting on sackcloth. Then the king's officers come to Modi'in to make the town sacrifice to idols. They go straight to him, because he's a leader in the town. Their offer is friendly: go first. Set the example. You and your sons will be counted among the king's friends, and rewarded with silver and gold. Everyone in town is watching what the priest does.
screen: `A TOWN, NOT THE CAPITAL.` → `A PRIEST AND FIVE SONS.` → `GO FIRST, AND BE THE KING'S FRIEND.`

segments.voice: He answers loudly, so the whole crowd hears. Even if every nation in the king's realm obeys and abandons the ways of its ancestors, I and my sons and my brothers will walk in the covenant of our fathers. Then the story turns violent. Another Jew steps up to offer the sacrifice the king demands. Mattathias, burning with zeal, kills him at the altar, kills the king's officer too, and pulls the altar down. The book compares him to Phinehas, the zealous priest in the book of Numbers. It's a hard scene, and some readers are uneasy with it; the book itself offers no apology. Then Mattathias calls out through the town for anyone zealous for the law and faithful to the covenant to follow him, and he and his sons flee to the mountains, leaving everything behind. Some later Hanukkah retellings put an older cry in his mouth, the call Moses made at the golden calf. In the King James words: "Who is on the LORD's side? let him come unto me." In Hebrew, mi la-Adonai elai. Then a turn that's easy to miss. Some of the faithful hide in the wilderness, the enemy attacks them on the Sabbath, and they refuse even to block the caves, because it's the Sabbath. They die, the text says, with their families. When Mattathias hears, he and his friends decide: if anyone attacks us on the Sabbath, we will fight back, or we'll all be wiped out. Refusing the king also meant choosing to stay alive, so the covenant would still have people to keep it.
screen: `I AND MY SONS WILL WALK IN THE COVENANT.` · `THE ALTAR PULLED DOWN.` · then, large: `WHO IS ON THE LORD'S SIDE?` · `FIGHTING BACK ON THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: say no to one wrong. Not with swords; with a sentence. Sit tall and let your breath slow down. Think of one small wrong you're being invited to join. A rumor at work, a shortcut that cheats someone, a joke at somebody's expense, a habit you've been going along with. Picture the moment the invitation comes, and everyone watching. Now hear yourself say no, calmly and clearly, in one short sentence. Say it a few times in your mind until it feels like yours. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Mattathias. The priest of Modi'in who refused the king's sacrifice, called the faithful to follow, and began the revolt. Today's word.
Your line: who is for the lord. Today, when you're invited to go along with something wrong, notice who is watching, and say your one sentence. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

fork.reveal: he answers out loud that he and his family will keep the covenant, then calls the faithful to follow him into the mountains.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Maccabee revolt began with an army.

what a scholar hears: 1 Maccabees 2 compares him to Phinehas and gives his own call; the Hebrew cry mi la-Adonai elai comes from Exodus 32:26 and later retellings.

893.title: Rededication
893.hook: Judah the Maccabee retakes the Temple and rededicates it
893.howItsDone: Jews celebrate Hanukkah for eight nights beginning on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, lighting one more light each night on a hanukkiah, with blessings, and often placing it where it can be seen from outside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mattathias said no out loud in Modi'in and called the faithful to follow. Your line was who is for the lord. Where did you say your one sentence? Today, his son walks back into the Temple. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

Weeds. That's one of the first things they see. Mattathias has died, and his son Judas, called Maccabeus, has led the fighters through battle after battle. Now, the first book of Maccabees says, they go up to Mount Zion to the sanctuary. And they find it desolate. The altar profaned. The gates burned. The priests' rooms pulled down. And shrubs growing in the courtyards, the text says, like in a forest or on a mountainside. The sanctuary itself, gone wild. The fighters tear their clothes, put ashes on their heads, and fall on their faces. Then they get up and do the next thing: Judas sends men to hold off the enemy in the fortress nearby, and chooses priests to start cleaning.
screen: `SHRUBS IN THE COURTYARDS.` → `THEY TEAR THEIR CLOTHES.` → `THEN THEY START CLEANING.`

segments.voice: The cleaning is careful. The defiled stones are carried out to an unclean place. Then a hard question: what about the old altar of burnt offering, which had been profaned? They decide to pull it down. But they don't throw the stones away. They store them on the Temple mount, the text says, until a prophet should come to show what to do with them. Remember the last page, a few days ago: prophecy had gone quiet. So they leave the question open, on a pile of stones, waiting. Then they build a new altar of whole, uncut stones, following the law. New holy vessels. The lampstand brought back in, the lamps lit. And early on the twenty-fifth day of the month Kislev, they offer sacrifice on the new altar, with songs, harps and cymbals, and keep the dedication of the altar for eight days with gladness. Judas and the people decide it will be kept every year, for eight days. That's Hanukkah. The word means dedication. It's the same Hebrew word the Torah uses when the altar of the tabernacle is first anointed. In the King James words: "This was the dedication of the altar." Notice what's not in the first book of Maccabees: a small jar of oil. That story is in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, which asks: what is Hanukkah? It tells of one jar of pure oil, sealed by the high priest, enough for one day, that burned for eight. Both stories are part of how Jews remember the holiday. One is about rebuilding with your hands. The other is about light that lasted longer than it should.
screen: `STONES KEPT FOR A PROPHET.` · `A NEW ALTAR, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `THIS WAS THE DEDICATION OF THE ALTAR.` · `ONE JAR OF OIL, EIGHT DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: clean something for fresh use. It doesn't need to be big. A mug, a desk, a candleholder, a shelf, a corner of a room you've stopped using. If you can, do it now, slowly; if not, choose it and picture yourself doing it. As you clean, notice what you're clearing away, and what you'd like this thing to be for from now on. Then take a breath and let it be new. If there's something you can't decide what to do with, set it aside, like those stones, and let the question wait. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to dedicate it. The bell holds the time.
Rededication. Cleaning the profaned Temple, building a new altar, and setting it apart again, eight days with gladness. Today's word.
Your line: rededicate. Today, take one thing that got neglected, a habit, a space, a friendship, and give it back its purpose. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

894.title: The Hasmoneans
894.hook: the rebels became kings, and later rabbis were wary of their power
894.howItsDone: Students of Pirkei Avot learn Hillel's warning, do not trust in yourself until the day of your death, and the Talmud's stories of King Yannai and of Yochanan the high priest are studied in tractates Kiddushin and Berakhot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, weeds in the Temple courtyards, a new altar, eight days of gladness. Your line was rededicate. What did you give back its purpose? Today, a harder question: what happens to rebels after they win? Day eight hundred ninety-four.

Words on brass. Near the end of the first book of Maccabees, the people of Jerusalem write their thanks on tablets of brass and set them up on pillars on Mount Zion. The tablets honor Simon, a son of Mattathias. The book is glowing about his years: the land had peace, it says, and every man sat under his own vine and his own fig tree, with no one to make him afraid. So the people make Simon their leader and their high priest. But they add a condition, written right into the decree: until a faithful prophet should arise. The family of Mattathias, the Hasmoneans, now holds the sword, the Temple and the government. The question the next chapters of Jewish history ask is what that much power does to a family of heroes.
screen: `THANKS WRITTEN ON BRASS.` → `EVERY MAN UNDER HIS FIG TREE.` → `UNTIL A FAITHFUL PROPHET ARISES.`

segments.voice: Years later. In the Talmud, the Hasmonean ruler is now called King Yannai, and he wears two crowns: the crown of a king and the crown of the high priest. Tractate Kiddushin tells a tense story. Yannai comes home from a victory and throws a feast for the sages of Israel. At the table, one guest stirs him up, telling him the sages resent him. Then an elder named Yehudah ben Gedidyah speaks up, with the whole room listening: King Yannai, let the crown of kingship be enough for you. Leave the crown of priesthood to the descendants of Aaron. The story says Yannai, furious, turns on the sages and kills them, and the world is left desolate of Torah until Shimon ben Shetach restores it. Remember who this family was. Mattathias's sons risked everything so that no king could force his will on the Temple. Their descendants end up as kings the sages feared. Some readers think that's why, when the Talmud asks what Hanukkah is, it answers with a jar of oil and the lights, not a throne. And another passage, in tractate Berakhot, tells of a high priest named Yochanan who served faithfully for many years and changed at the end. The Talmud ties it to Hillel's warning from Pirkei Avot: do not trust in yourself until the day of your death. Heroes can change. The power that rescues can become the power that crushes, sometimes within one family.
screen: `TWO CROWNS ON ONE HEAD.` · `LET THE KINGSHIP BE ENOUGH.` · `OIL AND LIGHTS, NOT A THRONE.` · then, large: `DO NOT TRUST IN YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to watch what power does to heroes, starting close to home. Settle and breathe. Think of a moment you had a little power: a promotion, being the oldest sibling, being the one who knew the password, being right in an argument. Did you use it the way you would have wanted when you had less? No need to judge. Just look honestly. Then think of one person you admire who now holds power, and wish them the wisdom of Yehudah ben Gedidyah's line: let one crown be enough. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to ask to stay faithful to who you were. The bell holds the time.
The Hasmoneans. The family of Mattathias, who rescued the Temple, and whose descendants became kings the rabbis were wary of. Today's word.
Your line: heroes can change. Today, when you have a little power over someone, use it the way you'd want it used on you. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

895.title: Many Judaisms
895.hook: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argue over law and Temple
895.howItsDone: Jews today belong to different movements and communities, such as Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others, and study the Second Temple sects through the Mishnah, the Talmud and the writings of Josephus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Yannai wore two crowns, and a sage told him one should be enough. Your line was heroes can change. How did you use your bit of power? Today, the arguments in Jerusalem multiply. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

One man in Jerusalem wants to find the right way to live, so he tries all of them. That's how the historian Josephus describes his own youth. There were, he says, three schools of thought among the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes. He went through all three, the hard way, from the inside. Then, still not satisfied, he went out to the desert and lived with a teacher named Bannus, who wore clothes made from what grew on trees, ate only what grew wild, and bathed in cold water day and night. Only after all that did he come back to the city and choose. His search tells us something on its own: in those days, being Jewish came in more than one shape.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN TRIES ALL THREE.` → `A TEACHER IN THE DESERT.` → `MORE THAN ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Josephus lays out the schools. The Pharisees keep many customs handed down from the fathers that are not written in the law of Moses, and they teach that souls live on after death. The Sadducees hold that only the written laws are binding, and say the soul does not outlive the body; Josephus says they were fewer in number but included people of high rank. The Essenes live in close communities and share their property in common, so that no one is rich and no one is poor among them. And Josephus adds a fourth group, followers of Judas the Galilean, who say God alone is their ruler and will call no man master. The Mishnah, the rabbis' own book, lets us hear two of these groups argue. In tractate Yadayim, the Sadducees complain to the Pharisees: you say holy scriptures make the hands impure, but the books the Mishnah calls Hamiram don't? Some readers take that word to mean Homer. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai answers, and the debate goes on, round after round, each side making its case. Notice the shape. These aren't people who've lost their faith. They're people who care so much about the Torah and the Temple that they argue about every detail: what counts as Torah, who should run the Temple, what happens after death, how to live. In those days, there were many ways to be Jewish, and the Mishnah keeps the Sadducees' complaint in their own words.
screen: `PHARISEES: CUSTOMS FROM THE FATHERS.` · `SADDUCEES: ONLY WHAT'S WRITTEN.` · `ESSENES: EVERYTHING SHARED.` · then, large: `SADDUCEES AND PHARISEES ARGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: respect a group unlike yours. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a group whose way is different from yours: another congregation, another denomination, another political party, a family down the street that keeps its customs differently, or no customs at all. Picture one actual person from that group, someone with a face and a name. Then ask: what do they care about so much that they'd argue for it? Find one thing in them you can honestly respect. You don't have to agree. Just let the respect be real. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Many Judaisms. Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others, all arguing over Torah and Temple in the same land at the same time. Today's word.
Your line: many ways then too. Today, when you meet someone who does your tradition, or any tradition, differently, ask one curious question before you decide anything. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

Josephus describes Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and a fourth group, and the Mishnah records arguments between them.
the Mishnah records Sadducees and Pharisees arguing with each other

896.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
896.hook: scrolls hidden in caves at Qumran, found in modern times
896.howItsDone: A synagogue may keep a genizah for worn-out books and pages that contain God's name, burying or storing them rather than throwing them away, and visitors to the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem can see some of the scrolls on display.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, and a young Josephus trying them all. Your line was many ways then too. What curious question did you ask? Today, some of those voices turn up in a cave. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

A stone goes into a dark hole in a cliff, and something inside breaks. That's the story usually told about how it started: a shepherd in the hills above the Dead Sea, looking for a stray animal, tosses a rock into a cave and hears pottery crack. Inside are clay jars. Inside the jars, rolled-up scrolls, written in Hebrew and Aramaic. More caves follow, near a place called Qumran, some holding scrolls, some only scraps. They had been sitting in the dark, in a dry desert, the whole time, waiting.
screen: `A STONE INTO A CAVE.` → `CLAY JARS, ROLLED SCROLLS.` → `WAITING IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Keeping writing in clay jars isn't a new idea, and the Tanakh itself describes it. In the book of Jeremiah, with Babylon at the gates, the prophet buys a field, and the deed is to be put away. In the King James words: "put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days." A clay jar, so the words last. In the caves near Qumran, scrolls turned up in clay jars too. Among the scrolls are copies of books of the Bible, written out by hand. And beside them are writings of a community's own: rules for a community that lived together and shared what it had, hymns, commentaries reading the prophets as if they spoke about the readers' own day. Some scholars connect that community with the Essenes Josephus described yesterday; others see it differently. Nobody knows for certain who hid the scrolls, or exactly why. Maybe for safekeeping in a dangerous time. Maybe as a resting place. Jewish tradition has its own word for that: genizah, a place where worn-out holy writings are put away instead of thrown out. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of Rabban Gamliel the Elder being brought a translation of the book of Job. He had the builder set it under a course of stones: out of use, but not thrown away.
screen: then, large: `PUT THEM IN AN EARTHEN VESSEL.` · `THE BIBLE, COPIED BY HAND.` · `A COMMUNITY'S OWN RULES AND HYMNS.` · `GENIZAH: HIDDEN, NOT THROWN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look at a picture of one. If you have a phone nearby, search for a photo of a Dead Sea scroll, and just look. Don't read the captions yet. Look at the lines of letters, the cracks, the dark edges, the places where the hand of the copyist pressed harder. Somebody sat and wrote this, letter by letter, and somebody else wrapped it and carried it into the dark. If you can't look one up, picture a clay jar with a rolled scroll inside, and the cave going quiet around it. Stay with the hands that made it. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to give thanks for those who kept the words safe. The bell holds the time.
Genizah. A place where worn-out holy writings are put away instead of thrown out, the word Jewish tradition uses for scrolls hidden away like those found near Qumran. Today's word.

Your line: hidden in caves. That closes a week that ran freedom to practice, she encouraged them, who is for the lord, rededicate, heroes can change, many ways then too. Today, keep one thing that matters somewhere safe. Day eight hundred ninety-six.
